Training perfects the voice.

How do you find representation? How do you negotiate? How do you win an audition? How do you truly inhabit a role, so that meaning, mood and intention ring true? That is the work of the month.
Finding representation, negotiating engagements, professional auditioning and self-presentation — the business of a singing life.
Role and repertoire preparation in the original language, so that mood, intonation and dramatic meaning are true — not merely performed.
Music theory and history — the bedrock that turns a fine voice into an informed, complete artist.

A cathedral city on the river Elbe in the heart of Germany, with its own opera house and an hour from Berlin, Leipzig and Hanover — capital of the German state of Saxony-Anhalt, with an eventful history of more than 1,200 years.

Ochre hills and olive groves between Pisa and the Mediterranean Sea — Puccini’s country, where he wrote by the lake at Torre del Lago. Here the month ends: a week of rehearsal in the warm light, and a concert before an Italian audience.

Emerging artists at the threshold — completing or just beyond their formal training, ready to make the leap into the profession. A small, hand-picked cohort, welcomed from anywhere in the world; the stage is in Europe.

Admission by selectionECP-Arts is deliberately exclusive. A maximum of ten places per edition, awarded after a personal review of recordings and résumé — and an interview. We would rather leave a place empty than fill it.
ECP-Arts does not represent artists and is not an agency. Instead, we become a trusted interface: those we train arrive prepared, ready and connected.
Agencies and houses come to recognise what an ECP-Arts singer brings to the room — a reputation earned through results, not a certificate.
iiDirect exposure to agencies at the final showcase

ECP-Arts is guided by an honorary board drawn from the opera profession itself — artist management, house leadership, musicology, media and international relations. Between them they have spent their working lives deciding which young voices get heard.

The board advises the company, not the individual singer. It guides ECP-Arts as a whole — the artistic standard we hold ourselves to, the shape of the curriculum, our bearing in the profession. It does not teach, does not run the day-to-day business and holds no share in the company.

Ten singers and a small teaching team. Some are here for the whole month, others come for a block of days — which is how the profession itself works: a coach arrives, works intensively, and moves on. Who teaches in which week is published before you arrive, so no part of your month is a surprise.
We engage people who still work in the profession — who coached a production last season, who sat in a pit, who prepared a singer for an audition that was won. What they teach is what they do.
iSinging lessonsIndividually, every morning. Technique, not repertoire management.
iiRépétiteur coachingDaily, at the piano. The work that decides whether an aria sits.

vThe professionAgencies, contracts, fees, taxes, self-management. The part no conservatoire teaches.
